title: Office and Productivity Suites
summary: The word processor, spreadsheet and presentation concepts exams test: editing shortcuts, relative and absolute cell references, the everyday spreadsheet functions, formula versus value, sort and filter, chart choice, presentation views, and common file formats.
learningObjectives: Recall the common editing shortcuts and the function-key actions used across office apps.
Tell a relative reference from an absolute or mixed one and predict how each changes when a formula is copied.
Choose the right spreadsheet function for a counting, lookup or conditional task.
Match a data set to a suitable chart type and name the main office file formats.

blocks.title: Editing shortcuts and function keys
blocks.markdown:
Shortcuts that work across almost every office app (use **Cmd** in place of **Ctrl** on a Mac):

| Keys | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl+C / Ctrl+X / Ctrl+V | copy / cut / paste |
| Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y | undo / redo |
| Ctrl+A | select all |
| Ctrl+B / Ctrl+I / Ctrl+U | bold / italic / underline |
| Ctrl+F / Ctrl+H | find / find and replace |
| Ctrl+S / Ctrl+P | save / print |
| Ctrl+Home / Ctrl+End | jump to start / end of document |

Useful function keys in a spreadsheet: **F2** edit the active cell, **F4** toggle the `$` in a reference, **F5** go to a cell or open the navigator, **F7** spell-check, **F12** save as.

blocks.title: Word processor and presentation essentials
blocks.markdown:
**Word processor.** Text is shaped with **styles** (a named set of formatting applied in one click), **find and replace**, **headers and footers**, **page layout** (margins, orientation, columns), **track changes** for review, and **mail merge** to produce many personalised letters from one template plus a data list. Save as **.docx** (or **.odt**); export to **.pdf** for a fixed layout that anyone can open but not easily edit.

**Presentation.** A file is a deck of **slides**. The main views are **Normal** (edit one slide), **Slide Sorter** / **outline** (reorder and see structure), **Notes** (speaker notes under each slide) and **Slide Show** (full-screen delivery). A **slide master** sets the common look; **transitions** animate slide changes and **animations** animate objects on a slide. Save as **.pptx** (or **.odp**).

blocks.title: Cells, values and references
blocks.markdown:
A spreadsheet is a grid of **cells** named by **column letter + row number** (`B4`). A cell holds either a **value** you typed or a **formula** that starts with `=` and computes a value; the sheet shows the result while the **formula bar** shows the formula.

When you copy a formula, its references shift unless you lock them with `$`:

- **Relative** `B4` — both parts shift. Copied one column right and one row down it becomes `C5`.
- **Absolute** `$B$4` — neither part shifts; always points at `B4`.
- **Mixed** `B$4` (row locked) or `$B4` (column locked) — only the unlocked part shifts.

Use an absolute reference for a fixed cell every row must divide by or multiply against — a tax rate, a grand total.

**Ranges** are written with a colon (`B2:B10`). Basic maths uses `+ - * /` and `^` for powers; order of operations applies, so use brackets.

blocks.title: Everyday functions
blocks.markdown:
| Function | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `SUM(range)` | adds the numbers in the range |
| `AVERAGE(range)` | mean of the numbers |
| `COUNT(range)` | how many cells hold **numbers** |
| `COUNTA(range)` | how many cells are **not empty** (any type) |
| `COUNTIF(range, test)` | how many cells match a condition |
| `MIN` / `MAX` | smallest / largest value |
| `ROUND(x, n)` | round `x` to `n` decimal places |
| `IF(test, a, b)` | return `a` when the test is true, else `b` |
| `VLOOKUP(key, table, col, 0)` | find `key` down the first column of `table`, return the value in column `col` of that row; `0` (or FALSE) means exact match |
| `HLOOKUP` | the same, searching across the first **row** |
| `CONCATENATE(...)` or `&` | join text: `=A2 & " " & B2` |

`COUNT` vs `COUNTA` is a favourite trap: `COUNT` ignores text and blanks, `COUNTA` counts everything that is not blank.

blocks.title: Sorting, filtering and charts
blocks.markdown:
- **Sort** reorders rows by one or more columns; always extend the selection to whole rows so the data stays aligned.
- **Filter** (AutoFilter) hides rows that do not match a condition without deleting them.
- **Freeze panes** keeps header rows or the first column visible while you scroll.

Choosing a chart:

| Chart | Best for |
| --- | --- |
| Column / bar | comparing categories |
| Line | a trend over time |
| Pie | parts of a single whole (few slices) |
| Scatter (XY) | relationship between two numeric variables |

A pie chart with many thin slices, or used to show change over time, is the classic wrong choice.

blocks.title: Worked example: a small order sheet
blocks.markdown:
Columns: **A** item, **B** quantity, **C** unit price, **D** amount, **E** flag.

| Row | A | B | C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | Pens | 12 | 5 |
| 3 | Files | 8 | 25 |
| 4 | Markers | 15 | 18 |

**Amount, relative reference.** In `D2` type `=B2*C2` → **60**. Fill down: `D3` becomes `=B3*C3` → **200**, `D4` → `=B4*C4` → **270**.

**Grand total, then a share with an absolute reference.** `D5 = SUM(D2:D4)` → **530**. In `F2` type `=D2/$D$5` and fill down; `$D$5` stays fixed, so `F2 = 60/530`, `F3 = 200/530`, `F4 = 270/530`.

**Flag with IF.** `E2 = IF(D2>=200,"bulk","small")` → `D2` is 60 so **small**; `E3` and `E4` are **bulk**.

**Count the bulk rows.** `=COUNTIF(E2:E4,"bulk")` → **2**.

blocks.title: Common confusions
blocks.markdown:
- **The cell shows the result; the formula bar shows the formula.** They are not two different values.
- **A relative reference moves when copied.** If a formula must always hit one cell, lock it with `$`.
- **`COUNT` counts only numbers; `COUNTA` counts any non-empty cell.**
- **`VLOOKUP` searches the first column of its table** and needs `0`/FALSE for an exact match; without it you can get a wrong "near" hit.
- **`.csv` is plain values only** — it drops formulas, formatting, multiple sheets and charts.
- **`.pdf` is for sharing a fixed layout, not for editing** later.
- **Sorting only the selected column** scrambles the rows; select the whole table.

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.markdown:
- Editing shortcuts are shared across apps: Ctrl+C/X/V, Ctrl+Z/Y, Ctrl+B/I/U, Ctrl+F/H, Ctrl+S/P, Ctrl+Home/End. In a sheet: F2 edit, F4 toggle `$`, F5 go-to, F7 spell-check.
- A formula starts with `=`. Relative `B4` shifts on copy; absolute `$B$4` never shifts; mixed locks one part.
- Functions: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT (numbers) vs COUNTA (non-empty), COUNTIF, IF, VLOOKUP/HLOOKUP (exact match needs 0), MIN/MAX, ROUND, `&` to join text.
- Sort whole rows; filter hides without deleting; freeze panes to keep headers visible.
- Charts: column/bar to compare, line for trend, pie for parts of one whole, scatter for two numeric variables.
- Formats: .docx/.xlsx/.pptx (or .odt/.ods/.odp); .csv is values only; .pdf is fixed layout.

blocks.title: Practice
blocks.markdown:
Give the answer and a one-line reason.

1. `=A$2*$B3` is in `C3` and copied to `E7`. Which parts of the reference change?
2. A range holds numbers, text labels and some empty cells. Which returns only the count of the numbers: `COUNT(range)` or `COUNTA(range)`?
3. You need the mean of `D2:D50`. Which function?
4. A formula must always divide by the tax rate in `G1`. How should `G1` appear in the formula?
5. Which chart type suits monthly deposits over two years?
6. Which key edits the active cell in place in a spreadsheet?
7. You save a multi-sheet workbook as `.csv`. What is lost?
8. `=VLOOKUP("KOL", A2:C40, 3, 0)` — what does the `3` mean, and what does the `0` mean?

flashcards.front: In a spreadsheet, how do B4, $B$4 and B$4 behave when a formula is copied?
flashcards.back: B4 (relative) — both column and row shift. $B$4 (absolute) — neither shifts. B$4 (mixed) — column shifts, row is locked; $B4 locks the column instead.
flashcards.explanation: F4 cycles a reference through the four lock states.

flashcards.back: COUNT(range) counts only cells containing numbers. COUNTA(range) counts every cell that is not empty, whatever the type.

flashcards.front: What do the last two arguments of =VLOOKUP(key, table, 3, 0) mean?
flashcards.back: 3 = return the value from the third column of the matched row. 0 (or FALSE) = require an exact match on the key, searched down the first column of the table.
flashcards.explanation: A non-zero/TRUE last argument does an approximate match and needs the first column sorted.

flashcards.front: Where do you see the formula, and where the result?
flashcards.back: The cell displays the computed result; the formula bar shows the underlying formula (which always begins with =).
flashcards.explanation: Press F2 to edit the formula in the cell.

flashcards.front: Which chart for: comparing categories, a trend over time, parts of one whole?
flashcards.back: Comparing categories — column or bar. Trend over time — line. Parts of one whole (few slices) — pie. Two numeric variables — scatter.
flashcards.explanation: Pie for a time series or many slices is the classic wrong choice.

flashcards.front: What is special about .csv and about .pdf as save formats?
flashcards.back: .csv holds plain comma-separated values only — no formulas, formatting, extra sheets or charts. .pdf fixes the layout for viewing/printing anywhere but is not meant for later editing.
flashcards.explanation: .docx/.xlsx/.pptx and .odt/.ods/.odp keep the full editable document.

flashcards.back: Producing many personalised documents from one template plus a data list (e.g. a name/address table), one output document per row.
flashcards.explanation: A word-processor feature, driven by a spreadsheet or database as the data source.

flashcards.front: Name the main presentation views and what each is for.
flashcards.back: Normal — edit one slide. Slide Sorter/Outline — reorder and see structure. Notes — speaker notes per slide. Slide Show — full-screen delivery.
flashcards.explanation: The slide master sets the shared look across slides.
